In [[algebraic geometry]] and [[commutative algebra]], a [[ring homomorphism]] <math>f:A\to B</math> is called '''formally smooth''' (from [[French language|French]]: ''Formellement lisse'') if it satisfies the following infinitesimal [[Lift (mathematics)|lifting]] property: 

Suppose ''B'' is given the structure of an ''A''-algebra via the map ''f''. Given a [[Commutative algebra|commutative]] ''A''-algebra, ''C'', and a [[nilpotent ideal]] <math>N\subseteq C</math>, any ''A''-algebra homomorphism <math>B\to C/N</math> may be lifted to an ''A''-algebra map <math>B \to C</math>. If moreover any such lifting is unique, then ''f'' is said to be '''[[formally étale morphism|formally étale]]'''.<ref name="four one">{{EGA|book=4-1| pages = 5–259}}</ref><ref name="four four">{{EGA|book=4-4| pages = 5–361}}</ref>

Formally smooth maps were defined by [[Alexander Grothendieck]] in ''[[Éléments de géométrie algébrique]]'' IV.

For finitely presented morphisms, formal smoothness is equivalent to [[Smooth morphism|usual notion of smoothness]].

== Examples ==

=== Smooth morphisms ===
All smooth morphisms <math>f:X\to S</math> are equivalent to morphisms locally of finite presentation which are formally smooth. Hence formal smoothness is a slight generalization of smooth morphisms.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02H6|title=Lemma 37.11.7 (02H6): Infinitesimal lifting criterion—The Stacks project|website=stacks.math.columbia.edu|access-date=2020-04-07}}</ref>

=== Non-example ===
One method for detecting formal smoothness of a scheme is using [[infinitesimal]] lifting criterion. For example, using the truncation morphism <math>k[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^3) \to k[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)</math> the infinitesimal lifting criterion can be described using the commutative square<blockquote><math>\begin{matrix}
X & \leftarrow & \text{Spec}\left(\frac{k[\varepsilon]}{(\varepsilon^2)}\right) \\
\downarrow & & \downarrow \\
S & \leftarrow & \text{Spec}\left(\frac{k[\varepsilon]}{(\varepsilon^3)}\right)
\end{matrix}</math></blockquote>where <math>X,S \in Sch/S</math>. For example, if<blockquote><math>X = \text{Spec}\left( \frac{k[x,y]}{(xy)} \right)</math> and <math>Y = \text{Spec}(k)</math></blockquote>then consider the [[tangent vector]] at the origin <math>(0,0) \in X(k)</math> given by the ring morphism<blockquote><math>\frac{k[x,y]}{(xy)} \to \frac{k[\varepsilon]}{(\varepsilon^2)}</math></blockquote>sending<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
x &\mapsto \varepsilon \\
y &\mapsto \varepsilon
\end{align}</math></blockquote>Note because <math>xy \mapsto \varepsilon^2 = 0</math>, this is a valid morphism of commutative rings. Then, since a lifting of this morphism to<blockquote><math>\text{Spec}\left(\frac{k[\varepsilon]}{(\varepsilon^3)}\right) \to X</math></blockquote>is of the form<blockquote><math>\begin{align}
x &\mapsto \varepsilon + a\varepsilon^2 \\
y &\mapsto \varepsilon + b\varepsilon^2
\end{align}</math></blockquote>and <math>xy \mapsto \varepsilon^2 + (a+b)\varepsilon^3= \varepsilon^2</math>, there cannot be an infinitesimal lift since this is non-zero, hence <math>X \in Sch/k</math> is not formally smooth. This also proves this morphism is not smooth from the equivalence between formally smooth morphisms locally of finite presentation and smooth morphisms.
